subject: History
topic: Revolt of 1857 — causes, centres, leaders, aftermath, GoI Act 1858
description: First War of Independence/Sepoy Mutiny of 1857: immediate and remote causes, major centres and leaders, British suppression, Government of India Act 1858 — SSC CGL/UPSC/IBPS PO standard.

questions.stem: The immediate trigger of the 1857 Revolt was the introduction of the:

options.option_text: Enfield rifle with greased cartridges — soldiers had to bite them; fat was alleged to be of cow and pig
Doctrine of Lapse — annexation of Jhansi and other states was the political trigger in 1857
General Service Enlistment Act — soldiers objected to being sent overseas (crossing the sea)
Income tax introduction — taxing Indian soldiers' pay was the final provocation in 1857

questions.explanation: IMMEDIATE CAUSE: Introduction of the new Enfield rifle (Pattern 1853) with greased cartridges. Soldiers had to BITE the end of the cartridge (paper-wrapped, greased) before loading. Rumours spread that the grease contained: COW FAT (beef tallow — offensive to Hindus) and PIG FAT (pork lard — offensive to Muslims). Both communities were outraged → refused to use the cartridges. ACTUAL GREASING: The cartridges WERE greased, but whether specifically with cow/pig fat or with beeswax and vegetable tallow is disputed. The perception mattered more than the reality. MANGAL PANDEY: on 29 March 1857 at Barrackpore, refused to use the cartridges, attacked British officers → was arrested, tried, executed on 8 April 1857 (34th Bengal Native Infantry). OFFICIAL REVOLT: 10 May 1857 at Meerut — 85 Indian sepoys refused cartridges, were court-martialled. Fellow sepoys freed them, killed British officers, marched to Delhi. OTHER CAUSES (remote): Doctrine of Lapse, Subsidiary Alliance, missionary activity, racial discrimination, economic drain. PYQ FREQUENCY: immediate cause of 1857 in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims — most commonly tested fact.

questions.stem: The leadership of the 1857 Revolt at Kanpur (Cawnpore) was provided by:

options.option_text: Nana Sahib (Dhundu Pant) — adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, denied pension by British
Begum Hazrat Mahal — she led the revolt at Lucknow (Awadh), not Kanpur
Bakht Khan — he led the revolt at Delhi along with the proclamation of Bahadur Shah Zafar
Tatya Tope — he was Nana Sahib's commander; associated with Kanpur/Jhansi but not the primary leader

questions.explanation: KANPUR (CAWNPORE): Leader = NANA SAHIB (Dhundu Pant). He was the adopted son of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II. After Baji Rao II's death in 1851, British refused to grant Nana Sahib the pension/title his adoptive father had received. CENTRES AND LEADERS OF 1857: (1) DELHI: Bahadur Shah Zafar II (proclaimed emperor) + Bakht Khan (military command). (2) KANPUR: Nana Sahib + Tatya Tope (his general). (3) LUCKNOW/AWADH: Begum Hazrat Mahal + her son Birjis Qadir. (4) JHANSI: Rani Lakshmibai (killed June 1858 at Gwalior). (5) BAREILLY: Khan Bahadur Khan. (6) ALLAHABAD/BANARAS: Maulvi Liaquat Ali. (7) FAIZABAD: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah (also known as the 'Fiery Maulvi'). TATYA TOPE: Commander-in-chief of Nana Sahib's forces; continued guerrilla warfare until 1859 when captured and executed. PYQ FREQUENCY: Kanpur = Nana Sahib in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims History — very commonly asked match.

questions.stem: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi joined the 1857 Revolt primarily because of:

options.option_text: The Doctrine of Lapse — Jhansi was annexed because her adopted son was not recognised as heir
The greased cartridge issue — she was a soldier's widow deeply affected by the religious insult
Subsidiary Alliance — Jhansi was forced to accept a permanent British garrison at her own expense
Revenue enhancement — the British doubled the land revenue demand on Jhansi's peasantry

questions.explanation: DOCTRINE OF LAPSE: Lord Dalhousie's policy — if a ruler died without a natural (biological) heir, the state would lapse to the British and could not be inherited by an adopted son. JHANSI: Maharaja Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi died in 1853 without a natural heir. He had adopted a son (Damodar Rao) just before his death. Rani Lakshmibai petitioned the British to recognise the adoption — REJECTED under the Doctrine of Lapse. Jhansi was annexed in 1854. RANI'S REBELLION: Initially she tried legal means; when the 1857 revolt broke out in Jhansi (June 1857), she took charge as the rebel leader. She died fighting at Gwalior on 17-18 June 1858. QUOTE attributed to her: 'I shall not give up my Jhansi!' HUGH ROSE (British commander): praised her as 'the most dangerous of all Indian leaders.' OTHER STATES LAPSED UNDER DALHOUSIE: Satara (1848), Jaitpur, Sambhalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854). PYQ FREQUENCY: Lakshmibai + Doctrine of Lapse in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: V.D. Savarkar's 1909 book titled 'The Indian War of Independence' gave the 1857 revolt its nationalist framing. What had the British primarily called it?

options.option_text: The Sepoy Mutiny — British dismissed it as a mere military rebellion of disaffected soldiers
The Great Rebellion — all British historians used this dignified term for the major uprising
The Hindu-Muslim Conspiracy — British blamed the two communities for jointly planning it
The Annexation War — British acknowledged it as a war against their annexation policies

questions.explanation: NAMES FOR 1857: (1) BRITISH VIEW: 'SEPOY MUTINY' — a limited military mutiny of disaffected soldiers, not a national uprising. Also called 'The Great Mutiny' or 'Indian Mutiny.' BRITISH HISTORIANS: Sir John Kaye, G.B. Malleson wrote pro-British accounts. (2) V.D. SAVARKAR (1909): 'First War of Indian Independence' — gave it a nationalist, anti-colonial framing. His book was BANNED by the British. (3) MARXIST/HISTORIANS: R.C. Majumdar called it 'neither the First, nor National, nor War of Independence' — argued it was largely limited to North India and had no unified national consciousness. (4) S.N. SEN: 'Eighteen fifty-seven' (official government of India publication). (5) NEHRU/MAINSTREAM: accepted 'First War of Independence' in spirit. WHY NOT A FULL NATIONAL UPRISING: Limited geographical scope (Bengal, most of South India, Punjab, Sind were largely uninvolved or actively helped the British). Many rulers (Scindia, Nizam of Hyderabad) sided with the British. PYQ FREQUENCY: names and interpretations of 1857 in UPSC Prelims, state PSC History — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: The Government of India Act 1858, passed in the immediate aftermath of the 1857 Revolt, transferred power from:

options.option_text: The East India Company to the British Crown — Secretary of State for India replaced the Court of Directors
The British Parliament to the Indian National Congress — early steps toward self-governance
The Governor-General to the Viceroy of India — upgrading the title without changing the authority
The Crown to the Indian princes — rewarding loyalist native rulers with administrative powers

questions.explanation: GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1858: the most consequential administrative change after 1857. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) EAST INDIA COMPANY ABOLISHED — its rule ended; all powers transferred to the BRITISH CROWN. (2) SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INDIA (SoS): a Cabinet minister in London, assisted by a 15-member Council of India. He replaced the Board of Control and the Court of Directors. (3) GOVERNOR-GENERAL BECAME VICEROY (correct that the title changed but this was a consequence, not the primary transfer). Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India. (4) ALL TREATIES, etc. of the Company became treaties of the Crown. INDIAN COUNCILS ACT 1861: further reforms — allowed Indians into the legislative councils (advisory); codified laws (IPC 1860, CPC 1859). OPTION A vs C: option C is partially correct (GG became Viceroy) but the PRIMARY transfer was Company → Crown, not just a title change. The full substance of option C is incomplete; option A is the correct complete answer. PYQ FREQUENCY: GoI Act 1858 in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims History — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which areas notably did NOT revolt in 1857, making the British suppression easier?

options.option_text: Punjab, most of Madras, Bengal, and Hyderabad — actively supported or stayed loyal to the British
Awadh, Kanpur, and Jhansi — these were the heartlands of the revolt, not loyal areas
Delhi, Meerut, and Bareilly — these were the initial outbreak centres of the revolt itself
Nepal and Afghanistan — these are foreign territories, not part of British India in 1857

questions.explanation: AREAS NOT AFFECTED (loyal or pacified quickly): (1) PUNJAB: annexed only in 1849; Sikh soldiers had been defeated by the same mutineer army in Anglo-Sikh Wars — many Sikhs actively helped the British suppress the revolt. (2) BENGAL PROPER (excluding soldiers): rural Bengal was relatively quiet; zamindars and educated class (proto-nationalists) mostly sided with the British. (3) MADRAS and BOMBAY PRESIDENCY: South Indian troops remained loyal. (4) HYDERABAD: Nizam was a loyalist — provided support to British. (5) RAJPUTANA PRINCES: most sided with British (received assurances their states would not be annexed). WHY THIS MATTERED: the loyal troops allowed the British to redeploy; Sikh soldiers who fought WITH the British were key to recapturing Delhi. IMPLICATIONS FOR BRITISH POLICY POST-1857: Queen Victoria's Proclamation (November 1858) — promised no further territorial annexation, respect for native customs and religions — an attempt to win back the loyalty of princes and common people. PYQ FREQUENCY: regions loyal in 1857 in UPSC Prelims, state PSC History — 1× per 2-3 years.

questions.stem: Queen Victoria's Proclamation of November 1858 was significant for Indian history because it:

options.option_text: Announced the formal end of EIC rule and promised equal treatment of Indians under British Crown governance
Granted India dominion status — the first step toward self-governance under the Westminster model
Declared the Hindu-Muslim communal divide a permanent fixture of British India's administrative policy
Transferred all judicial powers from British courts to Indian courts across the subcontinent

questions.explanation: QUEEN'S PROCLAMATION 1858 (read out by Lord Canning at Allahabad): key promises: (1) All powers of EIC transferred to the Crown — confirmed formally. (2) No further annexation of Indian territories — Doctrine of Lapse implicitly abandoned. (3) Respect for rights, customs, and religion of Indian subjects. (4) Equal treatment for all British subjects, 'whatever their race or creed.' (5) Promises of education and employment based on merit. REALITY vs PROMISE: racial discrimination continued in practice; Indians were mostly excluded from high ICS positions (Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian ICS officer in 1863, brother of Rabindranath). WHY SIGNIFICANT: marks the start of direct Crown rule (British Raj proper). The promises gave Indian nationalists a legal basis to demand rights — 'you promised equal treatment, now fulfil it!' DOMINION STATUS (option B): only came with the Indian Independence Act 1947. The 1858 Proclamation said nothing about self-governance or dominion status. PYQ FREQUENCY: Queen's Proclamation 1858 provisions in UPSC Prelims, SSC CGL, state PSC — 1× per 2-3 years.
